en: The Ritual Manual for the Recitation of the Seven-Crore Cundī Dhāraṇī,
translated by Amoghavajra Tripiṭaka Master:
If there are those who practice this dhāraṇī seeking its accomplishment, they must first bathe and wear clean garments.
Adorn the site of practice (*maṇḍala*) and install the principal deity. Regarding the ritual for preparing the site of practice according to one's means:

one should select an excellent location and construct an altar (*maṇḍala*) measuring four cubits. Dig a trench three cubits deep and remove all broken tiles, rubble, poor soil, hair, body hair, bone ash, charcoal, insects, ants, and the like.
Fill it with high-quality, pure earth and level it. If no poor soil was found during the digging, take the earth previously excavated and use it as fill.
If there is any excess, one should know that this ground is most auspicious and will swiftly bring accomplishment.
Take the *gomaya* from a cow that has not yet reached its destination, mix it with scented water and fine, pure earth to form a paste.

Recite the mantra of the Bodhisattva Aparājita twenty-one times to empower it, and then smear the altar. Having smeared it, next take the five purities and mix them together (the five purities being the liquid of *gomaya*, cow [dung]...).

With urine, curd, milk, and clarified butter, empower [the site] one hundred and eight times with the mantra of the Bodhisattva Aparājita, circumambulate it to the right, and smear it all over the altar.

Whether establishing [the altar] upon a mountain rock, in a multi-storied pavilion, or on a boat—at any place where sages and worthies have attained the Way—simply wipe it with the five pure substances, sit facing east, and form the mudrā of Aparājita. Press [it down].
Recite the mantra seven times over the center of the mandala to consecrate it.

Then, take small portions of various medicinal herbs, the seven precious gems, and the five grains, and bury them at the center of the mandala to a depth of one cubit (*hasta*). Place the medicinal herbs and the seven precious gems therein.

Next, take the original soil to fill the pit completely, leveling and smoothing it. Press down with the right hand while reciting the verse for the Earth Deity three times; this is the verse for awakening the Earth Deity.
It is said:
O Devaputra, you who protect us, regarding all the Buddhas, the Guides, you have practiced the supreme conduct and purified the pāramitās;
like one who shattered the hosts of Māra, you are the Lion of the Śākyas, the Savior of the World.
I, too, have subdued Māra; I draw the maṇḍala.
Recite the mantra of the Earth Goddess as follows: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ pṛthivīye svāhā*.
Having performed the empowerment by reciting the verses, one should then apply sandalwood paste to the nine sacred seats so that they appear like full moons.

Using new, clean vessels—such as those made of gold, silver, refined copper, conch shell, mother-of-pearl, jade, porcelain, wood, or other new materials—one should fill them with various foods and drinks, as well as excellent incense, flowers, lamps, candles, and *argha* perfumed water, and arrange them as offerings according to one's means. If...

When a lay or monastic bodhisattva seeking accomplishment enters the maṇḍala, they should first pay homage to the Buddha, repent, rejoice in the merit of others, entreat [the Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma], and make vows.
Having done so, they should take the vow of the bodhicitta precepts themselves. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ maitrīcittam utpādayāmi. One who possesses the bodhicitta is free from all grasping at a self, detached from the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, and free from the grasper and the grasped.
Because the nature of one’s own mind is originally unborn and empty by its very essence, it is equal to that of all Buddhas of the past.
"Since [the Buddhas] have generated the bodhicitta, I too shall do likewise"—this is called the self-vow for receiving the bodhicitta precepts.
By reciting this once while contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), one obtains the adornment of immeasurable, boundless, and unconditioned merit for the three karmas;
until reaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), this merit remains uninterrupted, swiftly extinguishing all karmic obstructions. This is the mantra.
One will swiftly attain accomplishment and behold the presence of the tutelary deity.

Just as in the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where the Bodhisattva Maitreya explained the merits of bodhicitta to the youth Sudhana, one should first take the vow of the bodhicitta precepts.

Then, sitting in either the full-lotus or half-lotus posture as one prefers, with the body upright and eyes closed, one should immediately form the mudrā of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mudrā*) and visualize the Mother Tārā in the sky.
Surrounded by seven koṭis of Buddhas filling the entirety of space, one should, while in meditative absorption, pay homage to all the Buddhas and to the Buddha-mother Cundī;
thereafter, having applied incense to the hands, one should form the mudrā.
The Samaya Seal of the Buddha Family:

With both hands joined in the hollowed-palms gesture (*śūnyahastapuṭa*), extend the two index fingers and bend them so that their tips rest against the side of the first phalanges of the middle fingers;
place the two thumbs beneath the roots of the two index fingers. Forming this seal at the heart, recite the mantra seven times.
Visualize the Tathāgata’s thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs as clearly as if they were before one's eyes.
The mantra is: Oṃ tathāgatānubhāvāya svāhā.
By binding this mudrā and reciting the mantra, one immediately awakens all Tathāgatas, who shall all protect, mindfully attend to, and empower the practitioner.
All karmic obstructions and hindrances are illuminated and touched by light, whereby they are entirely eliminated. One’s lifespan becomes long, and merit and wisdom increase.
The noble assembly of the Buddha Family protects and rejoices; in birth after birth, one remains free from all evil realms.
One will be born by transformation within a lotus and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is the Samaya-mudrā of the Lotus Family:
join the two hands with palms hollowed and bring them together, then extend the two index fingers, the two middle fingers, and the two ring fingers, while bending [the thumbs and little fingers].
Forming the mudrā in the shape of a lotus and placing it at the heart, recite the mantra seven times while visualizing the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara complete with all his marks and signs.
Then, scatter the mantra over the right side of the crown as follows:
Oṃ paṇamō nābhavāya svāhā. By binding this mudrā and reciting this mantra, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and all other Lotus-holders are immediately awakened;
the light of all Bodhisattvas shines upon and touches them, whereby all karmic obstructions are entirely eliminated. All Bodhi...
The Bodhisattva is always a virtuous friend.
For the Vajra Family Samaya-mudrā:
turn the left hand outward and place the back of the right palm upon the back of the left hand, with the thumbs and little fingers of both hands [interlaced].
Interlock the fingers together in the shape of a vajra and place them at the heart; visualize the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and recite the mantra seven times.
Then, perform the scattering mudrā with the left hand at the crown of the head; the mantra is as follows:
Oṃ vajranāvāya svāhā. By forming this mudrā and reciting this mantra, all the assemblies of Vajra-saints will be awakened;

they shall bestow their empowerment and protection, so that all karmic obstacles and transgressions are completely extinguished, and no suffering shall ever again afflict one’s body. One shall thereby attain...
The body is as firm and solid as a vajra.
Next, form the second root mudrā (for self-protection):
interlace the two hands with the palms facing outward; extend the two index fingers and the two thumbs straight upward, and this constitutes the recitation of the Mother’s heart mantra.
Regarding the five locations for the mantra and mudrā of the body— namely, the forehead, then the right shoulder, then the left shoulder, then the throat,
and finally the crown of the head— the mantra for scattering [the flowers] is: Oṃ kāmale vimale jvāle svāhā.
When binding the seal that protects the body, arouse a mind of great compassion and universally take as objects of focus the six realms and four modes of birth,
vowing that all sentient beings be adorned with the armor of the great vow and the firm vajra-mail, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Next, form the mudrā for the earth-bound stake (kīla).
Interlace the two hands with palms facing inward, extend the two thumbs, and join the two index fingers and two little fingers together, bending them.
Hook the left index finger like a hook and draw it three times; then, strike the ground once with the thumb while reciting the mantra once.
The mantra is: Oṃ cundini jvalaya svāhā.
By binding this mudrā and reciting this mantra to empower the boundary of the earth, [the ground] down to the water’s edge becomes like a vajra-throne.
The celestial Māras and all obstructing spirits shall not cause harm or affliction; with little exertion, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
Next, the reciter should visualize at the center of the maṇḍala a great eight-petaled lotus, upon which is a lion throne.
Upon the throne is a jeweled pavilion, from which hang various necklaces, silk banners, streamers, canopies, and rows of jeweled pillars draped with exquisite [ornaments].

Celestial garments surround [the space], fragrant clouds rain down everywhere with various flowers, celestial music is played, and there are precious vases, *argha* offerings, divine delicacies, and lamps made of *maṇi* jewels.
Even if there is no maṇḍala, one will achieve accomplishment simply by visualizing these in the sky.
Having performed this visualization, one should recite this verse.
By the power of my merit, by the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment, and by the power of the Dharma-realm,
I universally make offerings and abide [in this practice].
Having recited this verse, one then recites the mantra of the Bodhisattva Mahākāśyapa-garbha (Great Ākāśagarbha):
Oṃ gaganasvabhāva vajra hūṃ. By consecrating with this mantra through recitation,
all imagined offerings become identical to reality, and all the noble assemblies may partake of them.
Next, perform the seal of the precious chariot (*ratna-ratha*).
Interlace the two hands with the palms facing upward; place the two index fingers across one another and press them together, then use the two thumbs to pinch the base of the index fingers.
Visualize that the messengers of the Buddha-family (*buddha-kula*) are driving a seven-jeweled chariot, which travels through the air.
Then, having gone to the palace of Vairocana Buddha in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven at the summit of the Form Realm, one should recite the mantra seven times.
The mantra is: Oṃ tūru tūru hūṃ.
Through the recitation of mantras and the empowerment of mudrās, the seven-jeweled chariot is brought to the summit of the Form Realm;
there, the Buddha-Mother Cundī, surrounded by the eight great bodhisattvas and their retinues of holy assemblies, mounts the seven-jeweled chariot.
Next, perform the mudrā for inviting the chariot.
Following the previous mudrā, pull the middle finger toward the body with the thumb; this constitutes the seal. Recite the mantra seven times. The mantra is as follows:
Namaḥ siddhye dīkṣāṇām tathāgatānām oṃ vairocani jñānakāya svāhā.
Through the empowerment of reciting the mantra, the assembly of noble ones comes from their original lands and dwells in the air above the ritual site (*maṇḍala*).
Next, one forms the seal for inviting the principal deity (*iṣṭadevatā*);
[the deity] descends from the chariot onto the ritual site according to the first root seal previously mentioned, using the two thumbs...
With the body, recite the mantra three times.
The mantra is: Oṃ jali jvalini he he bhagavati svāhā.
Next, bind the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Aparājita.

To expel obstructors, interlace the two hands with the right over the left to form fists, extend the two middle fingers so their tips touch, and rotate it three times around the body counter-clockwise. While doing so, contemplate thus: "All obstructors, Vināyakas..."
May all evil spirits and ghosts flee far away; may the assembly of noble ones who have come not transgress their original samaya, but abide here out of great compassion, and grant your protection.
Namo samanta-buddhānām. Oṃ hulu hulu caṇḍāli ma.
Recite *ṅki svāhā*. Next, perform the mudrā for the boundary of the enclosure (*prākāra*).

Following the previous mudrā for the boundary of the ground, bend the right index finger, extend the left index finger, and rotate it three times to the right, moving it according to the heart’s intent.
From afar, it becomes a vajra fortress of adamantine solidity;
even the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not transgress it, let alone others who are difficult to subdue, such as vināyakas, venomous insects, or those with sharp fangs and claws, who cannot approach it.
The mantra is: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ jñānaprakāśāya svāhā. Next, form the mudrā for the net boundary of the upper direction.
Following the previous wall mudrā, extend the index fingers of both hands;
press the right over the left at their middle joints and interlace them. Thus it is accomplished. Recite:
Recite this mantra three times.
The mantra is: Oṃ jñānabandhara svāhā.
By reciting the mantra and performing the mudrā with empowerment, it immediately becomes a vajra-like net, firm, solid, and indestructible.
Next, form the mudrā for sealing the fire enclosure with the "Secret Stitch.
With the left hand covering the back of the right hand, interlace the fingers and extend both thumbs straight upward.
Then recite the mantra three times while circling to the right three times. Visualize that outside the vajra wall there is a surrounding blaze of vajra flames. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ āsaṃmudrini hūṃ phaṭ. By binding this mudrā and reciting this mantra, one achieves a great protective seal;
the secret seam will not be entered by any māras.
Next, form the argha mudrā.
Interlace the two hands with palms facing inward and extend the two middle fingers so that their tips touch.

Press the two index fingers against the backs of the two middle fingers, and let the two thumbs rest alongside the bases of the two index fingers; this constitutes the root mudrā, which follows the same procedure as the previous root mudrā.
Slightly bend both thumbs and insert them into the palms; this forms the *argha* mudrā. Recite the mantra three times.
The mantra is: Oṃ carye carye caryāṅga-pratīkṣāpāragavati. (Ding yi...)
*Phaṭ svāhā*. The practitioner visualizes the assembly of noble ones with perfect clarity,
imagining himself standing beneath the feet of the Buddhas and the noble host,
holding a seven-jeweled *argha* vessel filled with fragrant water to bathe the feet of the noble assembly by offering this *argha* water.
Therefore, the practitioner’s three karmas become pure, defilements are washed away, and karmic obstructions are extinguished.
Next, bind the mudrā of the Lotus Family.
Following the previous root mudrā, extend both index fingers toward the body and visualize that from this mudrā, [light] flows forth without end.
Offer a lion throne of [appropriate] measure to all the noble assembly;
each of these noble ones shall sit upon it. The mantra is: Oṃ kāmala svāhā.
By forming the seat mudrā, reciting the mantra, and making offerings to the noble assembly, the practitioner shall attain fulfillment in the ten stages and obtain the vajra-seat.
Next, form the bathing mudrā.
Following the previous root mudrā, press the tips of the two thumbs against the middle joints of the two middle fingers;
this constitutes the mantra, which is recited three times. The mantra is: Oṃ caḥ svāhā.
Visualize that from this mudrā, immeasurable rays of light stream forth;
within each path of light, visualize immeasurable precious *bhadraghaṭa* vases filled with celestial, wondrous scented water, which pours down to bathe all the noble assemblies.
Furthermore, visualize in the sky immeasurable celestial music making offerings to the Honored One, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all the noble assemblies.
By binding this mudrā and reciting the mantra, the practitioner shall before long attain the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā-bhūmi).
Next, bind the ointment (gandha) mudrā:
following the previous root mudrā, join the two thumbs flatly against the side of the lower joint of the right index finger to form it while reciting the mantra.
The mantra for the three recitations is:
Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā. Visualize that from this mudrā, immeasurable rays of light flow forth;
within each path of light, there are immeasurable celestial wonders.

By forming this mudrā and reciting this mantra while making offerings of clouds of ointment incense and powdered incense to the Honored Ones, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all the assembly of holy beings,
one shall realize the fragrance of the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of all Tathāgatas.
Next, form the Flower Mudrā.
Following the previous Root Mudrā, place the two thumbs flat against the lower joints of the left index fingers; this completes [the mudrā].
Recite the mantra three times. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ svāhā. Visualize that from this mudrā, immeasurable rays of light stream forth;

along each path of light, there are immeasurable clouds of various kinds of exquisite celestial flowers of water and land, forming an ocean of offerings to the Honored One, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the entire assembly of holy beings.
By forming this mudrā and reciting the mantra, one shall attain the samādhi of Great Compassion, achieve the benefit and happiness of boundless sentient beings,
and remain untainted by any calamities or misfortunes.
Next, form the incense mudrā.
Following the previous root mudrā, bend the right index finger to press against the tips of the two thumbs. Recite the mantra three times.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ vasaṭ hūṃ. Visualize that from this mudrā, immeasurable rays of light stream forth;

along each ray of light, there arise immeasurable clouds of sublime, spontaneously born celestial incense, which together form an ocean-like offering to the primary deity, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the entire assembly of noble ones.
By forming this mudrā and reciting the mantra, one shall attain the accomplishment of the Samādhi of the Pervasive Dharmadhātu.
Next, form the food-and-drink mudrā.
Following the previous root mudrā, press the tips of the two thumbs with the left index finger; thus one forms the third [mudrā] while reciting the mantra.
The universal mantra is:
Oṃ jñaḥ svāhā. Visualize that from this mudrā, immeasurable rays of light stream forth;
along each path of light, there are immeasurable celestial wonders.
By making offerings of various clouds and oceans of food and drink to the Honored Ones, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas, and to all the noble assemblies of clouds and oceans of food and drink,
one shall attain the food of Dharma-joy and the rapture of dhyāna, the supreme flavor of the three liberations, and the accomplishment of samādhi.
Next, form the lamp mudrā.
Following the previous root mudrā, pinch the tips of both index fingers against the tips of both thumbs;
then recite the mantra three times. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ ni svāhā. Visualize that from this mudrā, immeasurable rays of light stream forth;

along each path of light, there are immeasurable clouds and oceans of various lamps and candles made of the seven precious gems, making offerings to the Honored One, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the entire assembly of holy beings. One shall thereby attain [the desired result].
The light of the Prajñāpāramitā purifies the five eyes.
Next, recite this praise:
*Avatara jvalana śarada samālabhi*.
Gocara-praṇāma-bodhanavidhi-ājñapti-sarī-suni-cūli-śikṣā-siddhini-saramanti-nam bhava śamani svāhānti-sarva-praṇave tadyathā taṭa.
Śrīṇa sate avyaya-stambha-namaḥ-prasīda roga-taraya rathakari-kṣetra-vyūna-śubhi-nipātra-karaṇa-kṣiṇ.
Sampuṭa-siddha-tvaṃ jantima-rāga-pracaṇḍa-likhara-jñānini re nisa-te nakrodhu-dīśvara-śikhariya-sattvaṃ.
(Tāraṇīye svasti te namo vajriṃ dhaṅkīradamīye suralipūrvavannapra-veśaya siddhārīya vāruṇi ti-paśyati naḥ saṃśayam sata.)

Tara-siddhikari-bhūrya-mānu-rāga-sime nati-nanda-van satti-raṅka-śi-tta bha-gavati (Buddhamātṛ) jñānī-dhāraṇī-satva-tara-samapada.
Next, the method for arranging the syllables of the *dhāraṇī* of the *iṣṭadevatā* is explained:

from the crown of the head down to the feet, one visualizes each syllable of the mantra clearly and distinctly, with light streaming forth that illuminates sentient beings transmigrating through the six realms and four modes of birth, giving rise to deep compassion and bestowing peace and happiness.
By arranging the nine syllables of the *dhāraṇī* upon the practitioner’s body, it is thereby accomplished.
The body of the Tathāgata, empowered by the eight great bodhisattvas, is sealed with mudrās.

If one performs the four types of rites—namely, pacifying (śāntika), increasing (pauṣṭika), subjugating (vaśīkaraṇa), and magnetizing (ākarṣaṇa)—according to the four colors white, yellow, black, and red, one will accomplish the siddhi. To form this mudrā:
interlace the two hands with the palms facing inward; join the two thumbs, the two index fingers, and the two little fingers together, and extend them straight upward. Thus it is accomplished.
Visualize the syllable Oṃ placed upon the crown of the head; touch the top of the head with the thumb. Next, visualize the syllable La above the two eyes;
then visualize the syllable Li above both the left and right eyes, again touching them with the thumbs.
Next, visualize the syllable *tsu* placed upon the neck and touch it with the thumb.
Next, visualize the syllable *ri* at the heart and touch it with the thumb.
Next, visualize the syllable *zu* placed on the left and right shoulders and touch them with the thumb.
Next, visualize the syllable *ni* placed upon the navel and touch it with the thumb.
Next, visualize the syllable *svā* (sandhi form) placed upon both left and right thighs and touch them with the little fingers.
Next, visualize the syllable *HA* placed upon both calves; touch them with the little fingers.
By virtue of visualizing the mantra, forming the mudrā, and performing the empowerment, the practitioner’s body immediately becomes the body of the Tathāgata Mārīcī.
All karmic obstructions are eliminated, immeasurable merit, fortune, and auspiciousness are accumulated, and the body becomes adamantine (*vajra*).

If one can constantly focus the mind on the practice of visualization while maintaining the *bhūtakoṭi* (the essence of destruction), all *siddhis* will manifest before one, and one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Next, bind the root mudrā and recite the root mantra seven times; then, by releasing the mudrā from the crown of the head, one immediately attains bodhi.
The disciple takes a rosary of one hundred and eight beads, strings them according to the ritual rules, and anoints the beads with fragrant ointment.
Holding the rosary in the palms of both hands at the heart, he recites the mantra seven times to consecrate the rosary. The mantra for consecrating the rosary is as follows:
Oṃ vairocana-male svāhā. While performing this empowerment, place it upon the crown of the head and make this aspiration with body and speech:
"I now wish to perform the recitation; may the Honored One, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas empower and protect me.
May I swiftly attain the fulfillment of the *siddhi* sought according to my wishes. Then...

Thereafter, supporting the bead with the ring finger and thumb of the left hand, move the bead with the thumb and ring finger of the right hand in the *dharmacakra-mudrā* (gesture of teaching the Dharma) held before the heart while reciting. The voice should be neither too slow nor too fast;
the mind should be focused without distraction, visualizing oneself as identical to the body of the deity, complete with all marks and signs, and likewise [visualizing] the deity before oneself.
Within the maṇḍala, visualize the Seven Tārās clearly and distinctly, seated facing one another and surrounded by their retinues.
Each time you recite the syllable *svāhā*, move one bead; perform one hundred and eight or one thousand and eighty repetitions as the count for the recitation, always maintaining a fixed limit.
If the count falls short of one hundred and eight, it will not suffice for the attainment of the desired goal.
Having completed the full count of recitations for the *siddhi*, coil the rosary in the palms of the hands, place it upon the crown of the head, and make this vow, saying:
"By the merit of my recitation, may all sentient beings who practice authentic conduct swiftly attain the accomplishment of the superior, middling, and inferior *siddhis*.
Then, place the rosary in its casket, form the *samādhi-mudrā*, straighten the body, close the eyes, and clarify the mind.
Purify the mind so that within the chest of the body, it manifests brilliantly and perfectly clear, like the full moon, with pure and radiant light.
Arouse great diligence and resolve to attain realization; if you can apply yourself single-mindedly without indolence, you will surely behold the fundamentally pure mind.
Within this perfect clarity, visualize the syllable Oṃ, and arrange the remaining eight syllables spiraling clockwise upon the perfect clarity.
While remaining in meditative concentration, one must clearly perceive the syllables of the mantra; once stability is attained without distraction, one is in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā.
Thereupon, one should draw a perfect, bright lunar disc and then contemplate the meaning of the seed-syllable *akṣara*.
The syllable *Oṃ* signifies the three bodies (*trikāya*) and also the fact that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen (*anutpanna*). As for the syllable *A*:
The syllable *li* signifies that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing; the syllable *zu* signifies that the characteristics of all phenomena are unapprehendable;
the syllable *li* signifies that all phenomena are without birth or cessation; the syllable *li* signifies that all phenomena are stainless;
the syllable *zhun* signifies that all phenomena are without equal awakening; the syllable *ni* signifies that all phenomena are without grasping or abandoning. *Svāhā*.
The syllable *ḍa* signifies the meaning of the equality and ineffability of all phenomena. The syllable *ha* signifies that all phenomena are without cause;
because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, one attains non-arising and non-ceasing.

Because they are neither arising nor ceasing, one attains the non-apprehension of characteristics. Because there is no apprehension of characteristics, one attains the absence of birth and death. Because there is no birth...
Through cessation, one attains stainlessness; through stainlessness, one attains peerless awakening; through peerless awakening, one attains freedom from grasping and abandoning;
through freedom from grasping and abandoning, one attains equanimity beyond verbal expression;
and through equanimity beyond verbal expression, one attains the non-apprehension that accords with *prajñā*, taking this as the skillful means.
Entering the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*), one realizes the *dharmadhātu-tathatā*; having completed the recitation of this samādhi,
one should bind the root mudrā,
followed by the bathing mudrā.
Next, bind the mudrā of the five offerings.
Next, recite praises and offer arghya water.
Next, bind the āsamani (reconsecration) mudrā and rotate it counter-clockwise once to dissolve the boundary.
Next, perform the seal of the precious chariot (*ratna-ratha-mudrā*).
With the index finger, push outward against the tip of the middle finger to escort the Noble One back to his original palace. The mantra for this escorting is as follows:
Oṃ namo bhagavate ārya-avalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya svāhā.
Next, bind the samaya-mudrās of the three families, reciting each mantra once, and perform prostrations to the Buddha as before, followed by confession.
Rejoice, request [the Buddhas to remain], make vows, and dedicate the merit toward unsurpassed bodhi;

then, as you please, practice walking meditation, recite Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, seal stūpas and images, bathe śarīra relics, circumambulate clockwise, and contemplate the six recollections.
Dedicate this accumulation of merit toward the accomplishment of whatever siddhis you seek.
Next, the four types of rites—*śāntika*, *paustika*, *vaśīkaraṇa*, and *abhicāra*—are explained. Regarding the *śāntika* rite:

it seeks the extinction of sins, the turning away of obstacles, and the removal of calamities, malevolent spirits, diseases, imprisonment, shackles, pestilence, national disasters, irregularities in rain and drought, damage to crops by insects, the oppressive influence of the five planets upon one’s natal star, and the exhaustion of all afflictions, leading to liberation.

This is called the Peaceful Rite (*śāntika*). When performing this rite, one should wear white garments, face north, and sit in the auspicious posture (*bhadrapīṭha*) with the knees crossed and raised.
One should visualize the deity as white and offer white food, drink, fruit, incense, flowers, lamps, and ground coverings.
From the first day to the eighth day of the lunar month, one should recite the mantra three times daily and perform *homa* at night for the purpose of pacification.
The mantra for averting calamities is:
Oṃ cale cule cuḷe amukaṃ śāntiṃ kuru svāhā. (Recite this for another person, substituting the name of that individual.)

Regarding the *Bhusuku* (Puṣpaka) rites: for the attainment of longevity, official rank and honor, hidden treasures, abundance, intelligence, and the power of retention (*dhāraṇī*) without forgetfulness;

for the accomplishment of medicinal formulas, the vajra, and so forth; or for manifesting the forms of lions, elephants, horses, and the like through the empowerment of mantras—whichever of these three signs appears, one shall obtain the fruit according to whether the aspiration is superior, middling, or inferior, as detailed extensively in the *Susiddhi*.

It is taught that those who seek illumination and enter the caves of the asuras, as well as the caves of the eight classes of spirits and deities, shall all succeed in entering them and realize the stages of attainment and supernatural powers;
those who seek the perfection of the two kinds of provisions shall swiftly achieve unsurpassed bodhi—this is called the rite of augmentation (*puṣṭi*).
When performing this rite, one should wear yellow robes, face the east, and sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
Sitting and visualizing the deity as yellow, one should offer incense, flowers, food, fruits, lamps, and the ground, all of which are yellow.
From the eighth day to the fifteenth day of the month, one should recite the mantra three times daily and perform homa at night.
The mantra is as follows: [insert mantra].
Oṃ jale jale jvalini [name of person] puṣṭiṃ kuru svāhā.
If one wishes to cause all people who see him to give rise to a joyful heart and to be gathered [under his influence], this is the *vaśīkaraṇa* mantra.

To subdue and summon—whether male or female, including the eight classes of devas and nāgas, yakṣīs, and unruly spirits and ghosts—and to cause all enemies who perform harmful acts to turn their hearts toward joy, one should rely on the protection and empowerment of all Buddhas;
this is called the rite of summoning and endearing. One who performs this rite shall wear red clothing and face [the direction].
Squatting with both knees pressed together on the ground is called the "Wise Posture" (bhadra-pīṭha).
One should visualize that the deity, the offerings of incense, flowers, food, fruit, lamps, the ground, and so forth, are all red in color.
From the sixteenth to the twenty-third day, one should perform recitation three times daily and perform *homa* at night using the mantra for summoning (*ākarṣaṇa-mantra*). It is as follows:
Oṃ jaye jayavati jñāne (for such-and-such a person) vaśīkuru svāhā. Regarding the rite of *ābhicāruka*:

for those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), slandered the Mahāyāna sūtras, destroyed the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), acted as rebels against their sovereign, or disrupted the True Dharma—for such persons, one should generate profound compassion and perform the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
For the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), use donkey dung or the ashes of cremated corpses to smear the altar.
When performing this rite, wear black or green clothing and face south, squatting with the left foot pressing down upon the right.
Visualize the deity as being black in color—either black or dark blue—and devoid of fragrance. Offer flowers that are black or dark blue, as well as food, drink, incense, and flowers for worship.
Offerings such as sweets, lamps, candles, the ground, and so forth shall all be black or blue in color.
From the twenty-third day of the month until the end of the month, one should perform recitation during the two periods of midday and midnight, and perform homa at night, using the following mantra:
Oṃ jvala-jvalana-prajvālana hūṃ phaṭ.
Next, the method for painting the image of the Mother Jvālāmukhī is explained.
One should take uncut white wool cloth from which the hair has been removed, and first prepare a mandala on a clean wall.
One should offer *argha* water, food, and drink according to one's means. The painter should observe the eightfold precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) and remain pure while painting the image.
In the pigments, one must not use glue made from animal hide; the colors should be mixed in new vessels. One should then paint the image of the Mother of Buddhas, Tārā, whose body is yellowish-white.
The deity sits cross-legged upon a lotus flower, his body adorned with a halo.

He wears garments of light gauze like those of a Bodhisattva of the ten *pāramitās*, all white in color from top to bottom. Furthermore, he is draped in celestial robes and wears necklaces, shoulder-straps, and a crown;
on his arms he wears shell-bracelets, and on his wrists, sandalwood and jewel rings. His face has three eyes, and he possesses eighteen arms above.
The second right hand makes the gesture of preaching the Dharma; the third hand bestows fearlessness; the fourth hand holds a sword;
the fifth hand holds a jewel garland; the sixth hand holds a palm with a fruit;
the seventh hand holds a battle-axe; the eighth hand holds a hook; the ninth hand holds a vajra; and the second left hand...
The first hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel banner (*cintāmaṇi-dhvaja*); the third hand holds a blooming red lotus; the fourth hand holds a water jar (*kamaṇḍalu*);
the fifth hand holds a noose (*pāśa*); the sixth hand holds a wheel (*cakra*); the seventh hand holds a conch shell (*śaṅkha*); the eighth hand holds a vase of excellence (*bhadraghaṭa*);
and the ninth hand holds a lotus upon which rests a Prajñā-pāramitā manuscript. Below this, one should depict a pool of water, within which is the Nanda Nāga King.

To the left of the *uṣṇīṣananda* nāga king’s *śatapatra* lotus seat, paint the practitioner holding an incense burner, gazing up with reverence at the Noble Mother Cundī, who looks down compassionately upon the practitioner.
Above, paint two devaputras from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven; one is named Kusuda, holding a flower garland, descending from the sky.
Having made offerings to the sacred image, one should, according to one's capacity, invite seven times seven monks in the order of their seniority to partake of a meal.

One should request them to perform the ritual for opening the light (*prabhā-vivaraṇa*), offer prayers of aspiration (*pariṇāmanā*), and recite hymns of praise. Beneath the image, one should inscribe the verse on the origin of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-nidāna-gāthā*).

Then, taking the image into a secret chamber, one should perform secret offerings, covering the image with silk while reciting mantras. Once the recitation is finished, one removes the silk covering, gazes upon the image, pays homage, makes offerings, and continues the recitation.

Cover it all with silk and be careful not to let anyone see it. Why is this? If one receives the ritual manuals and the methods for painting images from a teacher, and then transmits these painted images to others, they may be seized by Māra; therefore, they must be kept strictly secret.
One fascicle of the Ritual Manual for the Recitation of the Mother of the Seven Koṭis of Buddhas.
Completed on the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month in the second year of the Ninpō era at the hour of Wei (10–12 a.m.). Written by Kakuei.
